title: Ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακά
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 1. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὑπὸ τῶν κακῶν τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδιώχθη ὡς ἀσθενῆ ὄντα· εἰς οὐρανὸν δὲ ἀνῆλθεν.
sentences.tr: Hypo tōn kakōn ta agatha ediōchthē hōs asthenē onta· eis ouranon de anēlthen.
sentences.l: By the bad things the good things were driven out, as being weak; and up into heaven they went.
sentences.i: The good things were driven off by the bad as being weak, and went up into heaven.
sentences.n: An abstraction becomes a character simply by taking the article: τὰ ἀγαθά, τὰ κακά — the Goods and the Bads. A neuter plural subject regularly takes a singular verb in Greek: ἐδιώχθη and ἀνῆλθεν are both singular. ὡς with a participle gives the alleged ground: 'on the grounds that they were weak.'

sentences.t: Τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ ἠρώτησαν τὸν Δία πῶς εἶναι μετ’ ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.tr: Ta de agatha ērōtēsan ton Dia pōs einai met’ anthrōpōn.
sentences.l: And the good things asked Zeus how to be with men.
sentences.i: The good things asked Zeus how they were to live among men.
sentences.n: πῶς εἶναι is an indirect question with the infinitive: 'how they were to be.' μετ’ is μετά with its final vowel elided before a vowel. ἠρώτησαν is plural, where the neuter plural subject took a singular verb in the line before; later Greek allows either, and this fable has one of each.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν ⟨μὴ⟩ μετ’ ἀλλήλων πάντα, ἓν δὲ καθ’ ἓν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐπέρχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Ho de eipen ⟨mē⟩ met’ allēlōn panta, hen de kath’ hen tois anthrōpois eperchesthai.
sentences.l: And he said ⟨not⟩ all together with one another, but one by one, to come upon men.
sentences.i: He told them not to come to men all at once together, but one at a time.
sentences.n: ⟨μή⟩ is Chambry's editorial supplement: angle brackets mark words he adds to the transmitted text, and without this one the sentence says the opposite of what the story needs. Where you see them, the Greek is a reconstruction. εἶπεν takes an infinitive of indirect command (ἐπέρχεσθαι). ἓν δὲ καθ’ ἕν, 'one according to one' — one at a time.

sentences.t: Διὰ τοῦτο τὰ μὲν κακὰ συνεχῆ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ὡς πλησίον ὄντα, ἐπέρχεται, τὰ δὲ ἀγαθὰ βράδιον, ἐξ οὐρανοῦ κατιόντα.
sentences.tr: Dia touto ta men kaka synechē tois anthrōpois, hōs plēsion onta, eperchetai, ta de agatha bradion, ex ouranou kationta.
sentences.l: For this reason the bad things come upon men continuous, as being near, but the good things more slowly, coming down out of heaven.
sentences.i: That is why bad things come upon men without a break, being close at hand, while good things come more slowly, descending out of heaven.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ, the great Greek balance — 'on the one hand … on the other' — usually best heard as a comma of contrast rather than translated. συνεχῆ is a predicate adjective, 'continuous,' where English wants the adverb 'continuously'; βράδιον is the comparative adverb, 'more slowly.' The second half has no verb: ἐπέρχεται is understood again.

sentences.t: Ὅτι ἀγαθῶν μὲν οὐδεὶς ταχέως ἐπιτυγχάνει, ὑπὸ δὲ τῶν κακῶν ἕκαστος καθ’ ἑκάστην πλήττεται.
sentences.tr: Hoti agathōn men oudeis tacheōs epitynchanei, hypo de tōn kakōn hekastos kath’ hekastēn plēttetai.
sentences.l: That good things no one quickly obtains, but by the bad things each man is struck day by day.
sentences.i: No one comes by good things quickly, while every man is struck by bad ones day after day.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form — 'the point is that…' — one of several closing formulas in the collection. ἐπιτυγχάνω takes the genitive of what one hits upon (ἀγαθῶν). καθ’ ἑκάστην is elliptical for καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν, 'day by day': Greek leaves the obvious noun out.
